Grade 5 · Unit 5.2

Gravity, Stars, and Sky Patterns

How do Earth’s motions, gravity, and distances create patterns we can observe?

On a clear night in Michigan, look up. Gravity, distance, and Earth’s motions explain what you can see. You will see why the Sun looks so bright, why gravity pulls things toward Earth's center, how Earth's spin makes day, night and changing shadows, and why different stars show up in different seasons.

In this lesson

  1. The Sun is a star, and distance affects brightness
  2. Gravity pulls down
  3. Shadows and day/night show a daily pattern
  4. Different stars appear in different seasons
  5. Review only: Moon phases
  6. Try it at home
  7. Check yourself
  8. Play: Shadow Tracker

Concept 1

The Sun is a star, and distance affects brightness

The Sun looks bright because it is much closer than other stars.

Analogy

Flashlight near/far

flashlight close to face and far away.

“The same flashlight looks brighter when close.”

Data

Star distances

Sun close, other stars far.

“The Sun is not the biggest star. It looks brightest to us because it is the closest star. Some far stars give off more light than the Sun, but they are too far away to look bright.”

In science, an argument is a claim plus the evidence that backs it up.

Say it as an argument: “The Sun looks brighter because ______, my evidence is ______.”

Concept 2

Gravity pulls down

Gravity is the pull that makes things fall. Earth’s gravity pulls objects down, toward Earth’s center.

Try it

Drop test

dropped ball and sideways toss.

“Both fall down. Gravity pulls down.”

You did this before / what is new: You may have seen drop tests with forces; now you write an argument that “down” means toward Earth’s center.

Predict first: If you toss a ball sideways, will it fall down like a dropped ball?

You need: a soft ball or bean bag.

  1. Drop the ball from shoulder height. Watch where it goes.
  2. Toss it gently sideways. Watch it curve.
  3. Toss it up. Watch it come back.

What you should see: All three come down. Gravity pulls toward the ground, which is toward the center of Earth.

Why it matters: It does not matter how you toss it. Gravity pulls toward Earth.

Diagram

Down direction map

a globe with arrows at the top, bottom, and sides, every arrow pointing to the center of the globe.

“Down means toward the center of Earth, wherever you stand.”

Data

Argument evidence

table with three toss tests: dropped, tossed up, tossed sideways. Each test ends “came back down.”

“No matter how I toss it, it comes back down.”

In science, an argument is a claim plus the evidence that backs it up.

Say it as an argument: “Down means ______, my evidence is ______.”

TestWhat happened
Droppedcame down
Tossed upcame back down
Tossed sidewayscurved and came down

Concept 3

Shadows and day/night show a daily pattern

Earth spins once each day; the side facing the Sun has day, and shadow length changes in a pattern.

A shadow is the dark shape a stick makes when it blocks the Sun’s light. Its length is how far it reaches from the stick’s base to its tip. A top view looks straight down, like a map.

  • 8:30 am: 34 cm (about 13 inches), west
  • 10:00 am: 20 cm (about 8 inches), northwest
  • 12:00 pm: 9 cm (about 3.5 inches), north
  • 2:00 pm: 18 cm (about 7 inches), northeast
  • 3:30 pm: 30 cm (about 1 foot), east
Try it

Globe and flashlight

globe and flashlight Sun.

“Turn the globe slowly. One side is day. One side is night.”

You did this before / what is new: You used day/night models in 1-C; now you add measured shadow data.

Predict first: When you spin the globe, will the lit side stay in the same place?

You need: a globe or ball, a flashlight in a dark room, a sticker for Michigan.

  1. Put the sticker on Michigan. Shine the flashlight on the globe.
  2. Turn the globe slowly counter-clockwise (the way Earth spins, seen from above the North Pole).
  3. Say “day” when Michigan is lit and “night” when it is dark.

What you should see: The flashlight lights half the globe all the time. Spinning moves your sticker from day to night and back.

Why it matters: It is Earth that spins. The Sun does not go around us.

Data

Shadow length

A 10 cm (about 4 inches) stick on a sunny spring or fall day in Michigan, with morning, noon, and evening shadows:

  • 8:30 am: 34 cm (about 13 inches), pointing west
  • 10:00 am: 20 cm (about 8 inches), pointing northwest
  • 12:00 pm: 9 cm (about 3.5 inches), pointing north
  • 2:00 pm: 18 cm (about 7 inches), pointing northeast
  • 3:30 pm: 30 cm (about 1 foot), pointing east

The 12:00 pm row is when the Sun is highest in the sky. By the clock in Michigan, that is usually a little after 12:00. A quick rule: 1 inch is about 2.5 centimeters.

“Shadows are long in the morning and evening. They are short near noon. The shadow points west in the morning, north around the middle of the day, and east in the afternoon, always away from the Sun.”

Real world

Michigan noon

a playground pole at noon and after school.

“The Sun’s position changes. The shadow changes too.”

Concept 4

Different stars appear in different seasons

Earth orbits the Sun once each year, so the night sky changes by season.

Diagram

Earth orbit and night side

Earth around the Sun with the night side facing different star groups.

“In winter, our night side faces one star group. In summer, it faces another.”

A constellation is a pattern of stars that people have named.

Try it

Constellation card sort

picture cards for Orion, Leo, Scorpius, Cygnus.

“Sort the cards by season.”

Orion
Leo
Scorpius
Cygnus (the Swan)
CardSeason (best seen in Michigan evenings)
OrionWinter (Dec–Feb)
LeoSpring (Mar–May)
ScorpiusSummer (Jun–Aug), low in the southern sky
Cygnus (the Swan)Fall (Sep–Nov). Also visible across Michigan in summer.

Cygnus is a prominent pattern in the northern sky. Its brightest stars make the Northern Cross.

Draw each constellation on a card, mix them, and sort. Sample answers use the page's chart.

Data

Provided monthly visibility chart

Dec–Feb: Orion; Mar–May: Leo; Jun–Aug: Scorpius (low in the southern sky); Sep–Nov: Cygnus (also visible in summer).

“Orion appears most in winter. Scorpius appears most in summer.”

Real world

Michigan winter night

a clear winter sky with Orion.

“In Michigan winter, Orion is easy to find.”

Concept 5

Review only: Moon phases

The Moon reflects sunlight and changes appearance; this is review, not a new grade-5 PE claim.

Try it

Ball and flashlight

ball as Moon, flashlight as Sun.

“Move the ball. Only the sunlit side shines.”

You did this before / what is new: You saw Moon cards in 1-C; this is review only.

Predict first: Where should the ball be, compared with the flashlight, to see it all lit? To see none lit?

You need: a ball, a flashlight in a dark room.

  1. Put the ball at arm’s length from you, with the flashlight behind you shining past you onto the ball: you see the full lit face (full Moon).
  2. Move the ball to your right or left, a quarter turn around you: you see half lit.
  3. Put the ball between you and the flashlight so the lit side faces away: you see almost none lit (new Moon).

What you should see: Only the half of the ball facing the flashlight shines. What you see depends on where you stand.

Why it matters: This is review. The lit half is always half; the angle changes what we see.

Diagram

Moon phases

crescent, half, full.

“We see different amounts of the lit side.”

A Moon phase is how much of the Moon’s lit side we can see from Earth. A crescent is a thin, curved slice of light.

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Build a shadow clock: mark a pencil’s shadow at several times and use it to tell approximate time. Criteria: at least three labeled marks, same stick, same spot. If the sky is cloudy, use the provided dataset to make the shadow-clock graph.

Try it

What you need

  • flashlight
  • foam ball
  • pencil or clay
  • paper
  • tape
  • string
  • small globe or ball
  • two small balls
  • meter stick (about 3 feet) or ruler
  • index cards

Safety: if a flashlight uses a coin cell, keep the cell taped shut and away from younger siblings; never use wall current; do not shine flashlights into eyes. For drop tests use soft balls, clear a floor or table zone, and never toss toward faces or devices.

Try it

What you do

  • Model day and night with a globe.
  • Measure or graph shadow data.
  • Test drops and tosses.
  • Sort constellation cards.
  • Review Moon phases with a ball and flashlight.
  1. Stick a pencil (about 19 cm, or 7 inches, long) upright in clay in a sunny spot. Mark the shadow’s tip with chalk at three times (10 minutes each).
  2. Label each mark with the time. Measure the length with a ruler.
  3. Drop and toss a ball three ways (10 minutes).
  4. Sort constellation cards by season (10 minutes).

Notice: The shadow is longest in the morning and evening and shortest around noon. It points away from the Sun.

Why it matters: A shadow clock shows the Sun moves in a pattern we can use to tell time.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but it is best to collect your own when you can.

Real observation log: On a sunny day, measure a pencil or stick shadow at several times, mark which way it points (use a compass or a landmark), and graph the lengths.

Provided dataset if it is cloudy: a 10 cm (about 4 inches) stick on a sunny day in about March or September in Michigan. In summer the noon shadow is shorter, and in winter it is much longer.

  • 8:30 am: 34 cm (about 13 inches), west
  • 10:00 am: 20 cm (about 8 inches), northwest
  • 12:00 pm (Sun highest): 9 cm (about 3.5 inches), north
  • 2:00 pm: 18 cm (about 7 inches), northeast
  • 3:30 pm: 30 cm (about 1 foot), east

Provided seasonal star chart:

  • Dec–Feb: Orion
  • Mar–May: Leo
  • Jun–Aug: Scorpius (low in the southern sky)
  • Sep–Nov: Cygnus (also visible in summer)

Child reads: “We can graph the shadow. We can graph the seasons.”

Near you: Michigan’s long winter nights and short summer nights show seasonal daylight changes; winter constellations differ from summer ones. On a clear winter night in Michigan, Orion is often easy to see. Michigan’s Headlands International Dark Sky Park near Mackinaw City is one place to see many stars.

What did you learn?

Words to know

Star:
A huge ball of hot gas that gives off light.
Sun:
The star closest to Earth.
Rotate:
To spin around an axis.
Orbit:
To move around another object.
Shadow:
A place where light is blocked.
Gravity:
Earth’s downward pull.
Apparent brightness:
How bright something looks from where we are.
Constellation:
A pattern of stars that people have named.
Axis:
An imaginary line through Earth’s center.
Data:
Information that is collected.
Tutor notes: misconceptions and pacing

Pacing: five 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “The Sun is bright because it is the biggest star.” Correct: it looks bright because it is close.
  • “Day and night happen because the Sun moves around Earth.” Correct: Earth rotates.
  • “Seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer.” Correct: tilt changes sunlight spread and day length.
  • “The Moon makes its own light.” Correct: it reflects sunlight.
  • “Gravity needs air to work.” Correct: gravity works even without air.
  • “Heavier objects always fall faster.” Correct: gravity pulls down on all objects; air resistance can change falling.
  • “Down is just toward the nearest ground.” Correct: down is toward Earth’s center.
  • “Stars turn off in summer.” Correct: Earth’s orbit changes which stars we see at night.

Limits and cautions:

  • Moon phases are review only and are not a new grade-5 idea.
  • Solar-system scale is not taught here; it belongs later in Unit 8.6.
  • Air resistance is mentioned but not deeply taught; the grade-5 argument is about the direction “down.”
  • Seasonal star visibility depends on latitude, clouds, and light pollution; the provided chart guarantees evidence even without night observing.

Connections: Builds on: 1-C Sky Patterns; K–5 Unit 0: How Science Works. Builds toward: 5.4 Earth’s Spheres, Water, and Communities; Unit 8.6 Gravity, Orbits & the Solar System; Unit 11 Earth in Space.
